title: Spring Play in a Tang Garden
medium: Handscroll; ink and color on silk

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, From the Collection of A. W. Bahr, Purchase, Fletcher Fund, 1947
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A long Chinese handscroll painted on silk with a garden scene of spring play, where figures spend leisure time among plants, with birds and cats among the details.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, culture, period (Qing dynasty), public-domain flag, credit line, tags (Birds, Cats) and image URLs read from the record

context: A handscroll in ink and color on silk, dated by the Met to the 18th century (Qing dynasty). Its title refers to a Tang garden, so it imagines an earlier age, and the record's tags mention birds and cats.

descriptions.k: This picture is very long, like a story you unroll. It shows a garden in spring. People play there. Birds and cats are in it too. What can you find? What would you play?
descriptions.g12: This painting is a handscroll, which is a long picture you open a little at a time. It shows play in a spring garden in China. Look for birds and cats among the plants. What do you think the people are doing? Which part do you want to look at longest?
descriptions.g35: A handscroll is a long painting kept rolled up, and a person unrolls only a small part at a time. This one, made in China in the 1700s, shows spring play in a garden from the Tang dynasty, a time long before. The artist is unknown. Look for the birds and cats in the garden. How does a scroll make you look differently than a framed picture?
descriptions.g68: Made in the 18th century, this handscroll imagines a garden of the much earlier Tang dynasty, a common move in Chinese painting that looked back to a celebrated past. A scroll is viewed in sections, so the scene unfolds like a journey rather than all at once. The record notes birds and cats among its details. How does this way of viewing change your experience, and why might artists revisit an earlier age?
descriptions.g910: This Qing dynasty handscroll presents leisure in a garden that is set in the Tang period, which suggests that the picture is as much about an idea of the past as about observed life. The format controls how we see it: sections appear one at a time, so time and movement become part of the experience. Small details, such as birds and cats, reward patient looking. What does a long, unrolled format do that a single view cannot?
descriptions.g1112: Spring Play in a Tang Garden reflects how Qing-period painters used scenes of the Tang past to explore ideals of leisure, elegance and refinement. The handscroll format turns viewing into a sequence, shaped by the viewer's pace, and the unidentified artist invites questions about workshop practice and the market for such paintings. Interpretations of such scrolls vary, and the image alone cannot settle them. How do format, subject and attribution frame what claims we can responsibly make?

teacherNote.context: A Qing dynasty handscroll that imagines a Tang garden. Handscrolls are viewed a section at a time rather than all at once.
directions: Have students make a mini scroll from a long strip of paper and draw a scene that unfolds across it.
Ask students to describe only one section aloud and see if others can guess the rest.
Discuss why artists painted earlier eras and compare with another artwork that looks to the past.
